summary:
Belize decriminalised same-sex conduct through the courts. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, struck down the colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law as unconstitutional in Orozco v Attorney General, the challenge filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in 2013. The Human Dignity Trust carries the case among its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a law.

Before the ruling the statute was rarely enforced, yet the expat reporting at hand argues it had fostered intolerance; a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking is cited as evidence of residual public hostility. The same reporting holds that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly, and the country has an organised advocacy organisation in UNIBAM, which brought the Orozco litigation.

Belize accepted 15 of 17 sexual-orientation and gender-identity recommendations in its 2018 UN Universal Periodic Review, the first CARICOM state to accept that many. The accepted pledges cover legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and the collection of SOGI data. Two rights-equality recommendations were 'noted' rather than accepted.

The detention axis is undocumented for Belize. The one prison-focused source in the inventory, a survey of LGBTQ prisoners worldwide, mentions Belize only through a navigation-box link and records no birth-sex-versus-identity housing rule, no trans housing units, and no solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Where a detained trans visitor would be placed is therefore unknown, and the absence of any recorded standard cannot be read as a protective one.
tangentialFactors:
Belize's decriminalisation and its diplomatic positioning are ahead of its regional peers: the 2016 judgment made it the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn an anti-sodomy law, and the 2018 UPR round made it the first CARICOM state to accept 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations. Both comparisons sit alongside the fact that two equality recommendations were noted rather than accepted.

The litigation ran a long arc, from Orozco's 2010 filing through the 2013 Belize City hearing to the August 2016 judgment. The social climate described in the sources does not track the legal change closely: the pre-ruling statute was rarely enforced while still breeding intolerance, and the 1998 cruise-docking protest shows hostility that outlasted the statute's practical force.

Nothing in the inventory attaches a trans-specific legal claim to the Orozco ruling. The judgment addresses same-sex conduct, not gender identity, document markers, facilities or care.
localsOnly:
UNIBAM, the organisation behind the Orozco challenge, remains the named organised body for LGBT Belizeans, and the constitutional route it used is the demonstrated avenue for legal change in the country.

For residents, the accepted UPR commitments translate into promised police training, promised SOGI data collection, promised legal reform and promised explicit anti-discrimination legislation. Implementation of those pledges is not evidenced in this inventory, so their delivery should be treated as unverified.

Two of the reviewed recommendations, both concerning equality of rights, were 'noted' rather than accepted, which marks the outer edge of the government's stated commitment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prison placement for trans detainees in Belize is unresolved: no source here states a housing rule, a segregation practice or a trans-specific unit, so the question cannot be answered from this inventory.

Legal gender recognition is not addressed by any source in this inventory. Whether a trans visitor or resident can amend a birth certificate, passport or other marker, and on what conditions, is not sourced here.

Discrimination protection on grounds of gender identity in employment is not carried by any source in this inventory, despite the UPR pledge to legislate explicit anti-discrimination measures.

No post-2016 enforcement data, arrest statistics or police guidance on the treatment of trans people is available in this inventory; the practical operation of the Orozco ruling for a trans person is unverified.

Whether the accepted UPR recommendations have been implemented, in whole or in part, is not sourced here.
